title: Aesopwui Khararchan: Translated Aesop's Fables & Moral Stories in Tangkhul
alternate_titles: Aesop's Fables Translated into Tangkhul Naga
subject: Fables, Children Literature & Moral Instruction
notes: Classic translation of Aesop's Fables into Tangkhul Naga by TLS. Includes beloved timeless animal allegories adapted with native flora, fauna, and idioms of the Tangkhul hills.

front_matter.title_page: Aesopwui Khararchan: Translated Aesop's Fables & Moral Stories in Tangkhul (1978)
front_matter.preface: The translation of Aesop's Fables by the Tangkhul Literature Society provided generation after generation of Tangkhul school children with lively didactic stories. The translator ingeniously mapped Aesop's animals to familiar Himalayan highland counterparts: the hare became 'ngachon', the tortoise 'shimhar', the wolf 'ngayen', and the fox 'sharu', preserving the universal moral truth of each fable.

chapters.title: Shimhar kala Ngachon (The Tortoise and the Hare)
chapters.summary: The boastful hare challenged by the slow but persevering tortoise in Tangkhul prose.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Khararchan 1: Thot akha ngachon kashap akha leisai. Ana kashikatha sha pupupli 'I thada khangachon pamei malei!' hoda aphasa mathaikhangasang leisai. Chitharan shimhar kacham akha rarlaga hang: 'Ngachon, na eina i race khaksa-u!' Ngachonna mania: 'Na thada kachut-kachut zatnao china ili khaksa-ra kaji?' Kha athum race phokserie. Ngachonna shongzali khangachon thotlaga 'Shimhar kashapli kachut; i thingphun ngachingli ngaphama-u' hoda pilakna. Kha shimharna kakhut machamla zatpingsanglaga, goal line-li khare vashukrie! Moral (Tuitam): Ningkazang eina chotkasana khangaraorap khuiye.
chapters.english_translation: A Hare was making fun of the Tortoise one day for being so slow. 'Do you ever get anywhere?' he asked with a mocking laugh. 'Yes,' replied the Tortoise, 'and I get there sooner than you think. Run with me and I will prove it.' The Hare was much amused at the idea of running a race with the Tortoise, but for the fun of the thing he agreed. The Hare was soon far out of sight, and to make the Tortoise appear very ridiculous, he lay down beside the course to take a nap until the Tortoise should catch up. The Tortoise meanwhile kept going slowly but steadily, and, after a time, passed the place where the Hare was sleeping. When the Hare awoke, the Tortoise was across the finish line! Moral: Slow and steady wins the race.
exercises: Summarize the story of the Tortoise and the Hare in three Tangkhul sentences.
Translate the moral 'Slow and steady wins the race' into Tangkhul.

chapters.title: Sharu kala Sakalu (The Fox and the Grapes)
chapters.summary: The cunning fox leaping for sweet grapes and declaring them sour when out of reach.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Khararchan 2: Sharu akha kachak kashaklaga ramkhangateili zatlakha, thingphunli shantuk-kahai sakalu (grapes) theitserie. Sakalu chi thik-thik kacha, chithei kaphā kala tui-ngapom kachuk theilaga sharu chi shashik thotna. Ana sakalu khukhavai kaphungli thuksange; kha vashuk mashuk-mana. Khani, kathum chuksa-ngasotlakha khikha phā mashuk-mana. Chitharan sharuna awui makhayor mathatlaga hang: 'Khai! Sakalu hi kakhui-kashasai! Ili kakhui thei shakkhavai ning maleimana!' hoda valakna. Moral (Tuitam): Phā-mashuk-khalangli kashikahai hoda hangkasa mi kachungsai.
chapters.english_translation: A famished Fox will tell you, if he can, of the sweet grapes that hung from a vine high on a trellis. He longed to reach them, but they were beyond his leap. He took a running start and jumped, but missed. Again and again he tried after the tempting morsel, but at last had to give it up. He walked off with his nose in the air, saying: 'I thought those grapes were ripe, but I see now they are quite sour.' Moral: It is easy to despise what you cannot get.
grammar_notes: Verbal attempt compound: 'chuksa-ngasotlakha' (having tried jumping repeatedly).
exercises: What rationalization did the fox offer for walking away?
Identify the Tangkhul words for leaping and failing to reach.

chapters.title: Avaikha kacham ngalanao kala Ngayen (The Boy Who Cried Wolf)
chapters.summary: The young shepherd crying wolf falsely and finding no one believes a liar even when telling the truth.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Khararchan 3: Mayarnaowon akhana kaphungli avaikha (sheep) kashun leisai. Ana shongfa khangayeili ngacham-kaza chiwui vang khanganoilaga hohe: 'Ngayen! Ngayen rarlakna! Avaikha shaksangie!' Village-wui mikumo thapup thingkot khuilaga khangachonli rarer; kha chithuili ngayen malei-mana, mayarnaowon china kanganrilaga pamye. Zingkum khani hithada saserie. Chitharan zingsho akha kashung-mashung ngayen rarlakna! Mayarnaowon china lungkashung eina hohe: 'Ngayen rarlakna! Khangachon milu!' Kha mikumo akhakhana mashursang-mana, 'A maningkachang tui hangye' hoda leisai. Chitharan ngayenna avaikha pupupli shaksangserie. Moral (Tuitam): Maningkachang mi kashung tui hangkhalangli khipana machotsang-mana.
chapters.english_translation: There was once a young Shepherd Boy who tended his sheep at the foot of a mountain near a dark forest. It was rather lonely for him, so he thought upon a plan by which he could get a little company and some excitement. He rushed down towards the village calling out 'Wolf, Wolf,' and the villagers came out to help him. He laughed at them when they found no wolf. This he did twice. At last, a real Wolf came out from the forest. The boy cried in earnest terror, 'Wolf, Wolf, please come!' But the villagers thought he was deceiving them again, and nobody came to his aid. Moral: Nobody believes a liar, even when he tells the truth.
grammar_notes: Temporal iterative: 'zingkum khani hithada saserie' (did so two or three times).
exercises: Discuss the social consequences of falsehood in traditional village governance.
Translate the moral lesson into Hindi and English.

chapters.title: Samayār kala Khachangnao (The Lion and the Mouse)
chapters.summary: The mighty lion sparing the tiny mouse, who later gnaws the hunter's ropes to free the king of beasts.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Khararchan 4: Samayār (lion) kashang akha thingphun ngachingli ngaphamsai. Khachangnao (mouse) kacham akhana awui mai-ngalungli ngachonkatlakha, samayārna awui khut eina khuikahaisai. Khachangnaona khamathān haikaphā salaga hang: 'Shiyankasang, ili huikhuilu! Thot akha i nawui khangachon sarap sara!' Samayārna kanganrilaga ali kashikahaiserie. Zingsho charakha ngaphalaga, hunterbingna samayārli rui kashang eina thuksangie. Samayārna khongyui eina hu-hu kashoklakha, khachangnaona rarlaga awui khani-eina rui chi kakor-khakserie! Samayār chi ngatorie. Moral (Tuitam): Kakatnaobingna kashangbingli khangachon sara kashap lei.
chapters.english_translation: A Lion was awakened by a Mouse running over his face. Rising in angry wrath, he laid his paw upon him with intent to kill him. The Mouse piteously entreated him: 'Spare me, O King! and I will surely repay your kindness.' The Lion laughed and let him go. Some time after, the Lion was caught in the net of the hunters. He roared with fury. The Mouse recognized his roar, ran to the net, and gnawed the ropes with his teeth until he set the king free. Moral: Little friends may prove great friends.
grammar_notes: Tangkhul rodent gnawing verb: 'kakor-khak' (to sever completely by gnawing).
Diminutive suffix '-nao' marking smallness/humility (khachangnao = tiny mouse).
exercises: Contrast the physical sizes and reciprocal deeds of the lion and the mouse.
How does Tangkhul grammar express unexpected assistance?

chapters.tangkhul_text:
Aesopwui Khararchan Kasakakhui:
1. Shimhar kala Ngachon (Tortoise & Hare) -- Ningkazang eina khangaraorap
2. Sharu kala Sakalu (Fox & Grapes) -- Phā-mashuk-kaji tui
3. Avaikha ngalanao kala Ngayen (Boy & Wolf) -- Maningkachang tuiwui kasham
4. Samayār kala Khachangnao (Lion & Mouse) -- Kakatnao khangachon
5. Huina kala Maiwui Sha (Dog & Reflection) -- Ningkacham makasaloo
6. Kazingramwui Vanao kala Khangaphei (Ant & Grasshopper) -- Zingsho kaphā tharan ot salu

The Mouse piteously entreated him: 'Spare me, O King! and I will surely repay your kindness.' The Lion laughed and let him go. Some time after, the Lion was caught in the net of the hunters. He roared with fury. The Mouse recognized his roar, ran to the net, and gnawed the ropes with his teeth until he set the king free. Moral: Little friends may prove great friends.
